questions.question: Explain the 'rain switch' that controls Africa's climate map: how convergence produces the continent's wet belts and subsidence its deserts, including the role of the temperature inversion.
questions.expected_answer: The switch is the vertical motion of the air. Convergence occurs where surface winds flow toward each other or into a low; the piled-up air can only escape upward, and as it rises it expands and cools adiabatically until its vapour condenses into deep cumulus and cumulonimbus, delivering convectional rain — hence the permanently wet Congo Basin and Guinea coast under the equatorial low, and the summer-rainfall interior of southern Africa. Subsidence is the reverse: air descending from aloft is compressed and warmed adiabatically so its relative humidity collapses and cloud dissolves, while at the surface it spreads outward as divergence. Subsidence also builds a temperature inversion, a layer in which temperature rises with height; because warm air sitting above cool air is completely stable, surface thermals rise into the layer, find themselves cooler and denser than their surroundings, and stop — the inversion is a ceiling that prevents cloud growth. Wherever subsidence is permanent, deserts result: the Sahara beneath the northern subtropical high, the Kalahari and Namib beneath the southern one. Latitudes between the wet equatorial belt and the dry 30-degree belts receive rain only when the rising side of the circulation migrates over them.

questions.question: Describe the ITCZ's annual migration and use it to explain why the Congo Basin has two rainy seasons, Zimbabwe and the Sahel only one, and why the outer regions are so exposed to drought.
questions.expected_answer: The ITCZ is the low-pressure trough where the south-east trades of the southern hemisphere converge with the north-east trades of the northern hemisphere, forcing air upward into a girdle of thunderstorms around the tropics. It follows the overhead sun with a lag of about a month, because the trades converge on the zone of strongest surface heating. In January it lies across southern Africa — over Angola, Zambia and Zimbabwe, brushing South Africa's far north — driving the southern summer rains; by July it has moved to about 15 to 20 degrees north over the Sahel, watering Senegal, Mali, Niger and northern Nigeria while southern Africa has its dry winter. Places near the equator, such as the Congo Basin and southern Uganda, are crossed twice each year, once as the belt moves north and once as it returns south, so they record a double rainfall maximum. Places near the belt's turning points, such as Zimbabwe and the Sahel, are reached only once, at its furthest excursion, giving a single summer maximum and a long dry season. Because those outer regions depend on the belt's maximum reach, any season in which the ITCZ stalls short or arrives weakly removes most or all of their rain — which is why their harvests are so vulnerable to drought.

questions.question: Account for South Africa's three contrasting climates — dry-winter wet-summer interior, arid west coast and humid east coast — using the Kalahari High and the two ocean currents.
questions.expected_answer: The interior is governed by the Kalahari High, the continental limb of the subtropical high-pressure belt. In winter the anticyclone is strong and its subsidence inversion lies below the crest of the escarpment, so moist maritime air cannot climb onto the plateau; the interior has cloudless, dry, cold weather. In summer intense surface heating weakens the high and lifts the inversion above the escarpment, so moist Indian Ocean air pours over the eastern rim and feeds the afternoon thunderstorms of Mpumalanga, Gauteng and the Free State — one anticyclone breathing seasonally gives the plateau its dry winters and wet summers. The west coast is shaped by the cold Benguela Current, upwelled from depth: air resting on cold water is chilled from below, gathers little vapour and becomes stable, so it can deliver fog but almost no rain — hence the Namib and the arid coast at Alexander Bay. The east coast is shaped by the warm Mozambique-Agulhas system: air resting on warm water is heated from below, loads up with evaporated moisture and becomes unstable, ready to rise and rain — hence humid, green Richards Bay at nearly the same latitude as Alexander Bay. Nearly identical latitudes with opposite currents produce opposite climates, proving the currents, not the latitude, are the control.
